definition.text: A way of managing land that grows trees together with crops or pasture on the same ground.

facts.text: It can yield timber, fruit, nuts, mushrooms, medicinal plants, animals and other products.
It is managed to make the most of helpful interactions between plants and animals, using the forest as a model, and is described as applied agroecology.
Benefits include higher farm productivity and profits, less soil erosion, wildlife habitat, more biodiversity and carbon sequestration, provided the farm is well managed.
Growing varied products such as fuelwood and medicinal plants makes farm income more secure.
Trees store carbon in soil and wood and can recapture some carbon lost when forests were cut.
It is most common on tropical smallholdings, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, and has spread to the US and Europe.
A survey of over 700 East African households found at least 50% had begun planting trees to adapt to climate change.
The term was coined in 1973 by forester John Bene, but the practice is millennia old.

definition.text: Growing strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges.

facts.text: Pruned tree leaves are spread over the crop to supply nutrients.
The hedges act as windbreaks, reduce erosion and suppress weeds with mulch and shade.

definition.text: Crops deliberately grown in the shade beneath a canopy of trees.

facts.text: Shade-grown coffee is a well-known example; shading cuts weeding costs and improves coffee quality.

definition.text: An organic agroforestry system, developed by Ernst Götsch in Brazil, that copies natural forest succession to build productive food forests.

facts.text: It relies on dense mixed planting of perennial and annual crops and on cutting fast-growing pioneer plants to build up nutrients.
Documented benefits include better water penetration, higher productivity on poor land and moderated soil temperature.

definition.text: Rows of trees or shrubs planted to slow the wind over and around crops.

facts.text: They raise yields by reducing crop drying and stopping plants from being blown over.
The USDA lists windbreaks as one of five temperate agroforestry practices.

definition.text: Growing high-value specialty crops under a forest canopy that is managed to give the right shade and habitat.

facts.text: It ranges from planting crops under timber trees to adjusting existing stands so their plants sell better.
In 1929 J. Russell Smith's book Tree Crops argued tree crops could replace cereals in animal feed and protect the environment.

definition.text: A low-maintenance way of producing food modelled on woodland, with layers of fruit and nut trees, shrubs, herbs, vines and perennial vegetables.

facts.text: Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest form of land use and remain common in the tropics as home gardens.
They are a significant source of income and food security for local people.
Robert Hart coined the term in the 1980s and adapted it to the UK's temperate climate.

definition.text: Applying agroforestry in towns, combining trees, shrubs and crops in gardens, parks and streets.

facts.text: Agroforestry on rooftop gardens can cut energy demand for cooling by up to 20%.
Because urban land is valuable, the opportunity cost of other land uses is a major constraint.

definition.text: A plant grown to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

facts.text: Cover crops help manage erosion, soil fertility, water, weeds, pests, diseases and wildlife on a farm.
They are often grown only to prevent erosion: roots anchor soil and the canopy slows raindrops and runoff.
A meta-analysis of 102 field studies found they raised topsoil organic carbon by about 10% and nitrogen by about 20%.
They reduce water pollution and take carbon dioxide out of the air.
Thick stands smother weeds, and some suppress weeds chemically through allelopathy.
In one study songbird densities were 7–20 times higher in cotton fields with a clover cover crop.
Effects on the next crop's water and yield vary, especially in semi-arid regions, and long-term profitability is uncertain.

definition.text: A cover crop grown to raise soil fertility, usually ploughed in before it matures.

facts.text: Green manures are commonly legumes, which are high in nitrogen and can supply what a crop needs.
This replaces nitrogen that conventional farms apply as chemical fertilizer.

definition.text: A crop grown to lure pests away from the valuable crop.

facts.text: Once pests gather, the small trap area can be treated or the pests physically removed.
Mustard and radish trap nematodes, cutting their populations by 70–99%.
